I think most people agree that governments should provide for human rights, but other than "you have the rights not to be murdered or robbed" I can't think of any others. If you were asked to come up with a definition for human rights, what would you say? I already know about "life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness", but that seems really vague to me and I can't imagine how that could used for laws and such.

For full disclosure, the reason I ask is because I was reading this thread where internet access as a human right was being discussed. Here is my post trying to make sense of it.

EDIT: If you guys could, if you think you have an answer, I would really appreciate it if you would reply to this post giving your answer and explaining your perspective a little bit. It doesn't have to be perfect I just really want to see your views on the matter and have a discussion. Thanks!

What do you mean "provide for human rights"? I don't understand that part. Some people subscribe to "positive rights" where the government should provide facilities to its citizens, like education, roads, etc. and other people subscribe to "negative rights", i.e. only interfere when someone's rights are getting infringed.

You touched upon an important aspect when you wrote "robbed". The issue is a bit broader than that. Robbing involves violence. Stealing does not. For the government to act to defend it, the constitution must also ratify property rights. In a capitalist economy, property rights are as important as right to life. A socialist economy does not recognize private property at all; they recognize personal property.

That's just for starters. As far as I'm concerned, there are no right or wrong answers. Figure out what makes best sense to you, and form a country with like-minded people.

A socialist economy does not recognize private property at all; they recognize personal property.

This always strikes me as a distinction without a difference and the only explanations I ever hear come off sounding like "personal property is what I have, private property is what you have" like it's trying some semantic argument to justify taking what you want from someone who has it.

I took it to mean that socialist economies recognize personal property like you home but do not recognize private ownership of capital. So by this definition a socialist economy would allow you to own a home but you couldn't own a factory.

I tend to agree with the definition as understood by Thomas Jefferson and Thomas Paine. Natural rights are those that are necessary for a person to achieve their potential. As long as those rights do not interfere with the rights of other's natural rights, they are absolute. They are not something benevolently granted to us by the state. They exist independent of any government. A person alone on an island has those rights inherently. He or she does not need someone with a gun to tell them they are free to speak, but they are free to speak as they wish.

If your rights can be achieved in isolation, then those are natural rights. You have the right to believe in your own version of god. You do not have a right to a pony, since that would require the hand of something outside of existence. You have the right to pursue happiness, and the right to pursue unhappiness. You do not have the right to expect someone to provide you with the tools needed to do so.

That's not to say that the state does not have the ability to give you those tools if the state chooses. It may be the best strategy for a society to survive. It's not, however, a natural right.

Human rights are a social construct. Obviously they do not actually exist in any quantifiable objective way, they are an idea much like many of the ideas of religion. The basic rule that you have what you can defend is the only absolute.

Countries/people around the world that do pay homage to the concept do not recognize the same rights. In much of Europe for example, healthcare is a right but the right to bear arms is not recognized. In America the right to healthcare is not recognized but the right to bear arms is. Fundamentally the largest divide is the so-called positive (what others must make available to you) and negative (what others may not take from you) rights.

While we've been living in at least a decade or two of "human rights politics" in practice what has essentially happened is that 'human rights' have become an excuse for the more powerful countries and organizations of the world to exert influence into the domestic affairs of smaller countries. These actions are based on their subjective interpretations of the concept, and they can change their interpretation of 'human rights' to suit an agenda easily.

An opposing idea to rights (at least negative rights) is the idea of social utility. That is, whatever increases net happiness and/or strength is acceptable.
The only right humans have is to think.
